clue.text: Not a crash helmet-more to do with the breeches

definitions.text: Not a crash helmet-more to do with the breeches

parts.words: Not a crash helmet-more to do with the breeches
parts.note: the cap here is not headgear for a crash but a small charge that goes off with a crash in the breech of a gun

explanation.surface: Someone clarifies that a piece of kit is trouser-related rather than protective headwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breeches' looks like trousers, but it is the plural of a gun's breech, where the firing cap sits; 'crash' is the bang it makes, not an accident.
explanation.definitionFit: This small explosive capsule ignited the charge in muzzle-loading firearms when struck by the hammer.

parts.note: an egghead is an intellectual, but here it means those at the head of egg production in the countryside

explanation.surface: Clever people living in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egg-heads' suggests intellectuals; here it is the people in charge of hens and eggs on a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who run farms raising hens, ducks and geese supply the eggs.

clue.text: One of those relations with a sense of proportion

definitions.text: One of those relations with a sense of proportion

parts.words: One of those relations with a sense of proportion
parts.note: the relations are mathematical relationships between quantities, not family members

explanation.surface: A sensible member of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' suggests relatives; it means numerical relationships, such as three to one.
explanation.definitionFit: The relationship of one quantity to another, such as 2:1, expresses proportion.

parts.note: a yard is an imperial measure, not part of the decimal system, so it is the opposite of metric

explanation.surface: A dull kind of garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yard' seems a garden but is the imperial unit, which is not metric; prose is the opposite of verse in metre.
explanation.definitionFit: Prose has no regular metre, so prosaic writing lacks verse rhythm.

parts.note: standing orders are a chamber's permanent rules, but here they are read as instructions to stand up

explanation.surface: A question about a time when the legislature has no procedural rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Standing orders are Parliament's rules of procedure; read literally, when there are no orders to stand, members are seated, and a session is so called.
explanation.definitionFit: A session of Parliament is a period when it is in session, its members seated.

indicators.note: a display shows things laid out afresh, so the letters are set out in a new order

parts.note: the possessive spelling supplies an S here

explanation.surface: A heap of earth covered in ferns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'display of' rearranges A MOUNDS into the fern genus.
explanation.definitionFit: Osmunda is the royal fern genus, a group of plants named in the plural as a genus.

parts.note: a young animal such as a fox or bear is a cub
a Cockney 'e is the word he with the H dropped, leaving only E

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a youngster is sturdily built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links the pieces to the definition; a solid with six square faces is built squarely.
explanation.definitionFit: A solid with six equal square faces is shaped with square sides throughout.

parts.note: a hogshead is a cask holding 52½ imperial gallons, and a hog is a pig, so the cask is a 'pig head'

explanation.surface: A stubborn man compared with a huge barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: A hogshead is a large cask of 52½ imperial gallons; swap hog for pig to get a word for stubborn.
explanation.definitionFit: Stubborn and unwilling to change one's mind, like a mulish animal.

clue.text: My stars, the way things: are going up and up!

definitions.text: My stars, the way things: are going up and up!

parts.words: My stars, the way things: are going up and up!
parts.note: 'my stars' is an exclamation of surprise but also points to the science of stars; prices going up are rising steeply

explanation.surface: An exclamation about soaring prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My stars' looks like mild surprise, but it is the study of the stars; things rising enormously do so in an extreme, star-high way.
explanation.definitionFit: Rising to enormous levels, as with distances measured by those who study the stars.

parts.note: a final demand from one state to another, after which fighting begins if it is refused; the Latin root means 'last'

explanation.surface: A remark about the final thing said before war broke out.
explanation.definitionFit: A final set of terms, whose rejection leads to hostilities, is literally the 'last' word in Latin.

clue.text: Return by bus? It can't be true!

annotationWithheld.why: Return by bus? It can't be true! (5): BOGUS is B(OG)US, GO reversed inside BUS, but no separate word gives GO; 'Return' would have to be both GO and the reversal signal
annotationWithheld.clue: Return by bus? It can't be true!

parts.note: Finnish reads as 'finny', having fins; Schubert wrote a famous song and quintet about a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A question about a composer's piece on a subject from Finland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finnish' points to Sibelius country, but it means finned: the subject is a fish, from Schubert's song and Quintet named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Schubert's song Die Forelle and the related Quintet take this freshwater fish as their subject.

parts.note: 13 refers to the answer to 13-across, the drink; houses selling that drink are pubs or taverns

explanation.surface: A clue that is simply a number and a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 13-across is BEER, so the clue reads 'beer houses', places for drinking and lodging.
explanation.definitionFit: Public houses or taverns where ale is served are known as beer houses.

definitions.meaning: a fishing village on the south coast of Devon, a county in south-west England
the liquid in a pint glass sits beneath the frothy head

explanation.surface: A scene of the sea washing over the Devon coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer is a village on the Devon coast, and ale is what lies under a frothy head in a glass.

parts.note: history is what is gone by, and an expert is a master, so this is a master of the bygone

explanation.surface: A specialist in historical studies.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means a skilled practitioner, but split it reads as a master of the past, a history expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A highly skilled person is called an old hand or adept, literally a master of what is gone.

parts.note: a G.I., an American soldier, is a Yank, so a Yank in action is doing something; physical jerks are sharp pulls rather than exercises

explanation.surface: An American soldier doing his morning exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Physical jerks' is old British slang for keep-fit exercises, but here it means tugging; a G.I. is a Yank, so the answer reads as 'Yank doing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling something with sudden sharp tugs is jerking it, and a Yank doing it gives the word.

definitions.meaning: French twenty-franc gold coins bore an emperor's head and name
three French rulers of that name numbered the First, Second and Third

explanation.surface: Counting out gold coins one by one.
explanation.definitionFit: Old French twenty-franc gold coins carried this name, as did three Emperors numbered I, II and III.

clue.text: One would be deucedly out of place in a decent university

definitions.text: One would be deucedly out of place in a decent university

parts.words: One would be deucedly out of place in a decent university
parts.note: split as a phrase meaning a wicked lecturer, who would not suit a good college; 'deucedly' hints at the deuce, the devil

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain sort of person would be terribly unwelcome at a good college.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'a bad don', a wicked university teacher. 'Deucedly' is old slang for 'extremely', but the deuce is the Devil, and Abaddon is the Biblical angel of the bottomless pit.
explanation.definitionFit: Abaddon is the destroyer angel of the abyss in Revelation, a devilish figure, as 'deucedly' signals.

clue.text: Paving that might have stopped Cleopatra's suicide

parts.words: that might have stopped Cleopatra's suicide
parts.note: Cleopatra died from the bite of a venomous snake, so a call for that snake to stop would have saved her

explanation.surface: A road surface that could somehow have changed ancient history.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as ASP HALT: Cleopatra killed herself with an asp, so had it halted she would have lived.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac-like bitumen surfacing is used for roads and paths.

clue.text: He evades the price of freedom by the window

indicators.note: evades means the pronoun escapes from inside the phrase, so its letters are taken out

parts.note: a payment for a captive's release is the ransom
taken as he, the pronoun spelt out

explanation.surface: A man dodges paying a kidnapper and escapes through the window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evades' removes HE from THE RANSOM. 'by the' is a link; a transom is a crossbar over a door, or the window above it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small window above a door, set on a horizontal crossbar, is called a fanlight in Britain.

clue.text: Crazy to stay here looking back

indicators.note: looking back says the two words together are read from the end to the start

parts.note: crazy means mad
to stay means to stop, as in stopping at a hotel

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it would be mad to remain in a place, glancing over their shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looking back' turns MAD STOP into POTSDAM. 'here' is the definition: the clue itself is the place, the German city near Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue names a location by pointing at itself, and the German city of the 1945 conference is that location.

definitions.meaning: a card game, also called twenty-one or blackjack
a temporary bridge carried on floating boats

explanation.surface: A round of the card game played on board ship.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a British card game like blackjack, and also a bridge laid across floating hulls.

parts.note: to heat wine or ale with spices is one sense; a Hebridean island off Scotland's west coast is the other

explanation.surface: A question about a hot, spice-growing island.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tropical spice island, but Mull is in the Scottish Hebrides; 'warm' with spices is to mull wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulled wine is warmed with spices, and Mull is an island of the Inner Hebrides.

parts.note: split into 'green' for grass and 'sleeves' for the fine linen of a bishop's sleeves

explanation.surface: The title of a well-known old English folk song.
explanation.walkthrough: Greensleeves is a Tudor ballad, but the answer is both a stretch of green grass and the fine linen of the 'lawn sleeves' worn by Anglican bishops.
explanation.definitionFit: Mown grass makes a green, and bishops' sleeves are made of a fine linen with the same name.

parts.note: A 1923 novel by Aldous Huxley, so the word goes with 'Hay' as a book title

explanation.surface: Someone is shocked to find hay has been reserved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hay booked' suggests a reservation, but means Hay as part of a book title: Aldous Huxley's novel Antic Hay.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic sense of the word is grotesque or bizarre, as in a clown's capers.

parts.note: Mark, as a first name, belongs to an American author; the Roman figures make a pair, as an archaic word for two

explanation.surface: A query about which version of a model is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark I or II' sounds like model numbers; it means the author Mark of that surname, and 'I or II' shows a choice between two.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word for two is also the pen name of Samuel Clemens, author of Huckleberry Finn.

parts.note: 17 is the destroying angel of the abyss, so the place he will certainly reach is the underworld

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person will succeed, and is reassured.
explanation.walkthrough: 17-across is ABADDON, the angel of the bottomless pit; read as 'a bad don', a wicked man is sure to go to the infernal regions.
explanation.definitionFit: The infernal abode of the damned is where a wicked man, or the angel of the abyss, ends up.

indicators.note: of says the letters come out of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A stream of honey made by bees from clover.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'cloveR HONEy'; 'A flow' is a river, the French Rhône.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhône is a major river flowing from Switzerland through France to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: A small drop is not enough

definitions.meaning: a deficit, an amount by which something falls below what is needed

explanation.surface: A small fall in figures means there is not enough.
explanation.definitionFit: A deficit is the gap by which supply falls below need, and read as two words it is a brief tumble.

clue.text: Wise week-ender husband of a proper woman ?

definitions.text: Wise week-ender husband of a proper woman

parts.words: Wise week-ender husband of a proper woman
parts.note: the wise king of Israel's name, plus the nursery-rhyme man who was born on Monday and buried on Sunday, married to the prim Mrs of that surname

explanation.surface: A description of a sensible man who married a respectable lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Solomon was the wise king; the nursery-rhyme Solomon Grundy lives one week, Monday to Sunday, and Mrs Grundy is the byword for prudish propriety.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme figure lives his whole life in a week, his first name means wisdom, and Mrs Grundy stands for prudery.
